title: No oracle needed
hookLine: ask diviners about things you can't know, never about whether to stand by a friend (Enchiridion 32)

lines: A FRIEND IN TROUBLE, LATE AT NIGHT.
cards: The call comes after midnight. A friend is in trouble, and they need someone to come. It's a moment when a small voice can start bargaining.
Is this a good idea? Maybe I should sleep on it. People in Epictetus' day had a more formal way to stall.
They went to a diviner, someone who read birds or the insides of a sacrifice, and asked what the gods advised. Epictetus doesn't mock the diviner. He just draws a line around what the diviner is for.

teach.h: LEAVE CRAVING AND DREAD AT THE DOOR.
teach.b: When you go to a diviner, Epictetus says, you don't know how things will turn out. That's why you came. But you do know what kind of thing it is.
If it isn't up to you, it isn't good or bad in itself. So leave your craving and your dread at the door, and go in as you'd go to any adviser. When should you ask?

teach.h: ASK ONLY WHAT REASON CAN'T ANSWER.
teach.b: The way Socrates did, he says: only when the whole question turns on what will happen, and reason and skill have nothing to offer. Will a voyage go well? Will a harvest come in?
Questions like those, fine. When shouldn't you ask?

teach.h: A FRIEND IN DANGER? NO NEED TO ASK.
teach.b: When a friend or your country is in danger and you ought to share it, don't ask the diviner whether to. Even if the signs say death, injury or exile, reason has already answered. You stand by your friend.
Then the greater diviner. Epictetus tells an old story about the god at Delphi, who, it was said, threw a man out of the temple because he had not helped a friend who was being killed.

teach.h: EVEN DELPHI SIDES WITH THE FRIEND.
teach.b: Even the oracle, in the story, sides with loyalty over omens. And a look back at the week, since today closes it: these things happen. Aim at the good.
My mind is mine. First, what follows. What the role asks.
Honestly, simply. And today: a duty doesn't wait for a sign.

how: Some people who practice Stoicism separate questions about outcomes, which they may research or ask about, from questions about duty, which they try to answer by reason without waiting for a sign.

o: a guide who settles which duty you owe a friend
someone who read birds or sacrifices for what lies ahead
a judge who settled disputes between neighbors

games.q: no oracle needed — tap the pairs.

s: Epictetus says never to consult a diviner
he limits it: only for questions reason and skill can't answer.
in the story Epictetus tells, Delphi expelled a man who failed to help his friend
even the oracle sides with loyalty over omens.

games.q: your friend is in danger, and standing with them may cost you. you're tempted to ask a diviner first. what does Epictetus say?
o: ask, and do whatever the signs say.
don't ask. reason already says stand by your friend.
wait until the omens look better.
games.why: even if the signs say death or exile, he says, reason has answered: you share your friend's danger.

practice: Think of one duty you've been putting off while you wait for some kind of sign: the right mood, a clearer feeling, someone else going first. Ask plainly whether it's a question about what will happen, or about what you owe.
If it's what you owe, let the waiting go, and picture the first step.

wordCard.voice: Diviner. The adviser Epictetus says to consult only when reason has nothing to offer; when the question is whether to stand by a friend, reason has already answered. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: a seer or diviner, the one Epictetus says to consult only when reason can't answer.

carryVoice: Your line: reason has already answered. A friend in trouble doesn't need an omen. Day three hundred sixty-four, and a week complete.
